messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos is a 54-year-old parole officer who has spent two decades monitoring and managing high-risk offenders on the streets of a large Southwestern city. Eleven months ago, during a routine compliance check at a halfway house, he was assaulted by two uniformed officers who mistook him for a parolee who had fled. Despite showing his badge and identifying himself repeatedly, he was shoved to the ground, had a knee pressed into his back, and was handcuffed and left face-down on the pavement for more than thirty minutes before a supervisor arrived and recognized him. His weapon was taken, his record of service ignored. The officers later claimed it was a “misidentification in a high-pressure situation,” and the department’s internal review ruled the incident “within policy.” No charges were filed, no apology given, and no disciplinary action taken against the officers.

From that moment, Carlos felt a profound sense of betrayal—not just by the men who had assaulted him, but by the institution he had served faithfully. He now believes that the system he dedicated his life to is fundamentally corrupt, that justice is a hollow promise, and that he was sacrificed because of his ethnicity and his role as a parole officer, which made him an easy target. These appraisals of injustice and institutional failure have become the lens through which he interprets nearly every interaction. When he is under stress at work—especially when he sees a parolee misbehaving or violating conditions—the old anger surges back, and the memory of that morning intrudes, fragmented and unreal. He finds himself pushing it away before he can fully recall the details; the picture is incomplete, like a series of still frames with missing reel. The story feels too extreme to be true, even though he knows it happened.

The heart racing that preceded the assault now returns unpredictably. When his own pulse picks up—during a confrontation, a tense phone call, or even while jogging on his usual trail—it triggers a cascade of threat monitoring. Carlos starts scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, especially in places that are quiet. Unusual silence now feels dangerous to him; he has become hypervigilant in the middle of the night, lying awake listening for the creak of a floorboard, certain something is about to happen. He startles easily, jumping when a car backfires or when a colleague claps him on the back without warning. These threat responses in turn amplify his memory intrusions: the more he scans, the more likely he is to catch a glimpse of a uniformed officer or a similar doorway, and the memory flashes back, incomplete and overwhelming. The memory feeds his belief that he was wronged by the very people he trusted, which loops back into scanning and avoidance.

At work, Carlos has begun to avoid certain duties. He volunteers for desk shifts, cites a vague “cramped neck” to turn down walking beats, and deliberately schedules home visits only in neighborhoods where he knows the local precinct commanders personally. His supervisor has noticed his reluctance and flagged it in a performance review, warning him that his effectiveness is slipping. Carlos tells himself he is being careful, but he knows the real reason: he cannot bear the risk of being disarmed and humiliated again. The cycle tightens as his avoidance reduces his exposure to normal situations, making the anticipation worse each time.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a panic attack two weeks ago, triggered by a silent waiting room at the county courthouse. He sat alone for five minutes, his heart pounding, convinced someone was about to grab him from behind. He left without seeing his client and drove home shaking, unable to explain to his wife why his hands were clammy. That evening, he told her he was “losing his mind.” She convinced him to call a therapist. Carlos is terrified that he will never feel safe again, and he is equally afraid of losing the career that has defined him. He hopes that talking to someone will help him make sense of what happened—will give him back the piece of the story that feels missing—but he is not sure he can trust anyone enough to tell the full truth.

violation_explanations: Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that triggers (e.g., parolee misbehavior, silent waiting room) directly cause or strengthen Carlos's negative appraisals about systemic corruption; instead, triggers lead to memory or threat, then to appraisals.
Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette states appraisals are a lens but does not show them directly causing memory intrusions; the immediate cause is stress or triggers.

Negative Appraisals → Triggers: There is no causal link shown from his beliefs about injustice to the identification or creation of triggers; his appraisals influence interpretation but not explicitly cause triggers.
Memory → Threat: The memory is described as overwhelming but not directly causing a sense of threat; threat arises from triggers and scanning, not from the memory itself.
Threat → Negative Appraisals: Feeling threatened does not directly lead to his beliefs about systemic corruption; instead, threat loops through memory to reinforce appraisals.
